Switch with Pattern Matching

SWITCH WITH PATTERN MATCHING

A switch statement/expression that uses a selector expression whose type is a reference type, except String and enums, is called a switch statement/expression with pattern matching.

A switch that uses a selector expression whose type is byte, char, short, int, plus their wrapper types, and String, or enums, is a regular switch, i.e. a switch without pattern matching.

SWITCH STATEMENT (WITHOUT PATTERN MATCHING) RULES SUMMARY

Old Syntax ( : ) New Syntax ( -> )
Allows zero or more individual statements or zero or more code blocks.

Examples (all valid): 
case 0:

case 1: stmt1; stmt2;

case 2: { <code block1> } { <code block 2> }
 Allows either exactly one statement or exactly one code block.

Examples (all invalid): 
case 0 -> //invalid, empty case

case 2 -> stmt1; stmt2; //invalid, more than one statement

case 4 -> { } { } //invalid, more than one block
Selector expression type Limited to: byte, short, int, char, and their wrappers, String, and enum
Not Allowed: boolean, long, float, and double. 		Limited to: byte, short, int, char, and their wrappers, String, and enum
Not Allowed: boolean, long, float, and double
Case label constant type Must be compatible with selector expression type Must be compatible with selector expression type
case label Allows a single case constant. Allows multiple case constants separated by comma. Example: 
case 1, 2 -> { }
default label Not required Not required
case null Allowed in Java 21 only if the switch statement is exhaustive and follows the rule for dominance of case expressions. Allowed in Java 21 only if the switch statement is exhaustive and follows the rule for dominance of case expressions.
Order of switch labels No restriction No restriction
break Needed only to prevent fall through Prohibited when a switch label is associated with a single statement.

Allowed within the code block associated with a switch label but is redundant.
yield Not allowed Not allowed
exhaustive Not necessary Not necessary

SWITCH EXPRESSION (WITHOUT PATTERN MATCHING) RULES SUMMARY

Old Syntax ( : ) New Syntax ( -> )
Allows one expression or one code block. Requires yield to cause it to return value.

Examples: 
case 0: yield 1; //valid, returns 1

case 3: yield "aa".length(); //valid, returns 2.
case 2: "a".length(); //syntactically valid, no yield required for non-void method call but falls through without returning a value

case 1: 1; //invalid, missing yield keyword
 Allows one expression or one code block. No yield required for single expression but required only within code block.

Examples: 
case 1 -> 1; //valid, returns 1, no yield required
case 3 -> "aa".length(); //valid, returns 1, no yield required
case 4 -> { yield 1; } //valid, yield is required in a block

case 0 -> //invalid, missing expression
case 2 -> yield 1; //invalid, must not write yield
Selector expression type Limited to: byte, short, int, and char and their wrappers, String, and enum
Not Allowed: boolean, float, long, and double 		Limited to: byte, short, int, and char and their wrappers, String, and enum
Not Allowed: boolean, float, long, and double
Case label constant type Must be compatible with selector expression type. Must be compatible with selector expression type.
case label Allows a single case constant. Allows multiple case constants separated by comma. Example: 
case 1, 2 -> 1,
default label Not required if already exhaustive Not required if already exhaustive
case null Allowed in Java 21 but must follow the rule for dominance of case expressions. Allowed in Java 21 but must follow the rule for dominance of case expressions.
Order of switch labels No restriction No restriction
break Prohibited Prohibited
yield Required to return value Required only when returning a value from a code block. Otherwise prohibited.
exhaustive Necessary Necessary

SWITCH STATEMENTS AND EXPRESSIONS (WITH PATTERN MATCHING) RULES SUMMARY (JAVA 21 ONLY)

Old Syntax ( : ) New Syntax ( -> )
Selector expression type All reference types are allowed All reference types are allowed
Type of case constants Must be compatible with the type of the selector expression Must be compatible with the type of the selector expression
exhaustive Necessary Necessary
default label Not required if already exhaustive Not required if already exhaustive
case null
May appear anywhere except after default label.

try-with-resources

try-with-resources

You need to know the following points regarding try-with-resources statement for the exam:

  1. The resource class must implement java.lang.AutoCloseable. Many standard JDK classes such as java.io.FileInputStream implement the older java.io.Closeable interface, which was made to extend java.lang.AutoCloseable in Java 7.
  2. AutoCloseable has only one method: public void close() throws Exception.
  3. Resources are closed at the end of the try block and before any catch or finally block.
  4. Resources are not even accessible in the catch or finally block. For example: 
    try(Device d = new Device()) {
   d.read();
} finally {
   d.close(); // This will not compile because d is not accessible here.
}
    Note that try-with-resources was enhanced in Java 9 and it now allows you to use a variable declared before the try statement in the try-with-resources block. In this case, the variable is accessible after the try block, but the object referred to by it has already been closed: 
    Device d = new Device();
try(d) { // valid since Java 9
   ...
} finally {
   d.close(); // this compiles but may not work correctly because d is already closed.
}
  5. Resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration in the try clause.
  6. Resources are closed even if the code in the try block throws an exception.
  7. java.lang.AutoCloseable's close() throws Exception, but java.io.Closeable's close() throws IOException.
  8. If the code in the try block throws an exception and an exception is also thrown while closing a resource, the exception thrown while closing the resource is suppressed. The caller gets the exception thrown in the try block.
  9. If no exception is thrown from the try block but multiple resources throw exceptions while being closed, the caller gets the exception thrown by the resource that was closed first, that is, the last resource declared in the try-with-resources block. The rest of the exceptions are suppressed.
  10. Suppressed exceptions can be retrieved from the main exception by calling Throwable[] getSuppressed().
  11. AutoCloseable resources that you want the try clause to manage must be final or effectively final.
Unmodifiable collections

Unmodifiable collections using of/copyOf and Collections.unmodifiableXXX methods

  1. java.util.List and java.util.Set have of and copyOf static factory methods that provide a convenient way to create unmodifiable lists/sets.
  2. The of methods accept either an array or multiple individual parameters. If you pass it a collection, it will be treated as a regular object, that is, it will return a list/set containing the same collection object instead of returning a list/set containing the objects that the passed collection contains.
  3. The copyOf, on the other hand, accepts only a Collection. It iterates through the passed collection and adds all the elements of that collection in the returned list/set.
  4. Here are a few important points about these methods:
    1. They return unmodifiable copies of the original List/Set. Thus, any operation that tries to modify the returned list throws an java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException.
    2. The list/set returned by the copyOf methods is completely independent of the original collection. Thus, if you modify the original collection after passing it to copyOf, those changes will not be reflected in the list returned by the copyOf method.
    3. They do not support null elements. Thus, if your array contains a null and if you try to create a List using List.of, it will throw a NullPointerException.

Collections.unmodifiableXXX methods

  1. java.util.Collections also has several variations of unmodifiableXXX static methods such as unmodifiableList(List), unmodifiableSet(Set), and unmodifiableMap(Map). These methods return an unmodifiable view of the underlying collection.

    The fundamental difference between Collections.unmodifiableXXX and List.of/copyOf methods is that Collections.unmodifiableList returns a view instead of a copy into the underlying list. Which means, if you make any changes to the underlying list after creating the view, those changes will be visible in the view.

    Further, Collections.unmodifiableList has no problem with nulls.
  2. The word unmodifiable in unmodifiableXXX means that you cannot modify the view using a reference to the view.
Deadlock, Starvation, and Livelock

Deadlock, Starvation, and Livelock

The exam needs you to understand and differentiate among Deadlock, Starvation, and Livelock. The following are brief descriptions taken from Oracle Java Tutorial, which is sufficient for the exam:

  1. Deadlock describes a situation where two or more threads are blocked forever, waiting for each other.

    For example, two threads T1 and T2 need a File and a Printer. T1 acquires the lock for the file and is about to acquire the lock for the Printer but before it could acquire the lock, T2 acquires the lock for the Printer and tries to acquire the lock for the file, which is already held by T1.

    So now, both the threads keep waiting forever for each other to release their locks and neither will be able to proceed.
  2. Starvation describes a situation where a thread is unable to gain regular access to shared resources and is unable to make progress.

    This happens when shared resources are made unavailable for long periods by greedy threads. For example, suppose an object provides a synchronized method that often takes a long time to return. If one thread invokes this method frequently, other threads that also need frequent synchronized access to the same object will often be blocked.
  3. Livelock: A thread often acts in response to the action of another thread. If the other thread's action is also a response to the action of another thread, then livelock may result.

    As with deadlock, livelocked threads are unable to make further progress. However, the threads are not blocked. They are simply too busy responding to each other to resume work.

    For example, after acquiring the File lock, T1 tries to acquire the Printer lock. Finding the Printer lock to be already taken, it releases the lock for the File and notifies T2. At the same time, T2 tries to acquire the File lock and seeing that it is already taken, it releases Printer lock and notifies T1.

    This process can go on and on, both the threads releasing and acquiring the locks in tandem but none of them getting both the locks at the same time. So neither of the threads is blocked but neither of the threads is able to do any real work. All they are doing is notifying each other.
JAVA DATE FORMATTER

JAVA DATE FORMATTER — OCP CHEAT SHEET

BIGGEST TRAPS

  • M = month      m = minute
  • d = day-of-month      D = day-of-year
  • H = 24h clock      h = 12h clock

CORE PATTERNS

  • y = year
  • M = month
  • d = day of month
  • D = day of year
  • e = day of week
  • H = hour (0–23)
  • h = hour (1–12)
  • m = minute
  • s = second
  • S = fraction of second
  • z = time-zone name

LENGTH RULES

1) NUMBERS

1 letter → minimum digits, no padding
2 letters → zero-padded if needed

Examples:

d   -> 3
dd  -> 03
M   -> 7
MM  -> 07
H   -> 5
HH  -> 05

2) TEXT

< 4 letters → short text
4 letters → full text
5 letters → narrow text

Examples:

MMM   -> Jul
MMMM  -> July
MMMMM -> J

3) NUMBER/TEXT SWITCH

For M and e:
1–2 letters → number
3+ letters → text

Examples:

e    -> 2
ee   -> 02
eee  -> Tue
eeee -> Tuesday

FAST MEMORY

y M d D e H h m s S z
year, Month, day, Day-in-year, weekday,
24h, 12h, minute, second, fraction, zone

EXAM REMINDERS

  • Uppercase vs lowercase matters
  • Pattern length changes output
  • M/m, d/D, H/h are classic traps
  • z = zone name
  • S = fraction, not seconds
JAVA 21 SWITCH EXHAUSTIVENESS

JAVA 21 SWITCH EXHAUSTIVENESS — CHEAT SHEET

// 1) Expression => always exhaustive
int a = switch (e) { ... };

// 2) Statement on legacy type => may be non-exhaustive
switch (str) { ... }

// 3) Statement with pattern or null label => must be exhaustive
switch (obj) {
    case String s -> ...
    default -> ...
}

// 4) Enum: all constants => exhaustive, default optional
switch (color) {
    case RED -> ...
    case GREEN -> ...
    case BLUE -> ...
}

// 5) Sealed type: all permitted subtypes => exhaustive, default optional

// 6) default does NOT catch null
switch (obj) {
    case null -> ...
    default -> ...
}

// 7) Guarded case does not by itself satisfy coverage
case String s when ...
SERVICE PROVIDER RULE

SERVICE PROVIDER RULES

  1. If a service provider explicitly declares a public constructor with no formal parameters, or implicitly declares a public default constructor, then that constructor is called the provider constructor.
  2. If a service provider explicitly declares a public static method called provider with no formal parameters, then that method is called the provider method.
  3. If a service provider has a provider method, then its return type must:

    (i) either be declared in the current module, or be declared in another module and be accessible to code in the current module;
    and
    (ii) be a subtype of the service specified in the provides directive;

    or a compile-time error occurs.
  4. While a service provider that is specified by a provides directive must be declared in the current module, its provider method may have a return type that is declared in another module.

    Also, note that when a service provider declares a provider method, the service provider itself need not be a subtype of the service.
  5. If a service provider does not have a provider method, then that service provider must have a provider constructor and must be a subtype of the service specified in the provides directive, or a compile-time error occurs.
Garbage Collection Notes

GARBAGE COLLECTION NOTES

  1. An object can be made eligible for garbage collection by making sure there are no references pointing to that object.
  2. You cannot directly invoke the garbage collector. You can suggest the JVM to perform garbage collection by calling System.gc().
  3. Note that objects pointed to by static variables of a class are not collected even when all objects of that class are collected because those variables belong to the class and not to the instance of the class.

    They are garbage collected only when the class itself is unloaded by the class loader.
Duration / Period toString

DURATION / PERIOD TOSTRING

The following is from JavaDoc API description of the toString methods of Duration and Period.

Duration.toString

It generates a string representation of the duration object using ISO-8601 seconds-based representation, such as PT8H6M12.345S.

The format of the returned string is PTnHnMnS, where n is the relevant hours, minutes, or seconds part of the duration. Any fractional seconds are placed after a decimal point in the seconds section. If a section has a zero value, it is omitted. The hours, minutes, and seconds all have the same sign.

Examples:

"20.345 seconds"               -> "PT20.345S"
"15 minutes" (15 * 60 sec)    -> "PT15M"
"10 hours" (10 * 3600 sec)    -> "PT10H"
"2 days" (2 * 86400 sec)      -> "PT48H"

Note that multiples of 24 hours are not output as days, to avoid confusion with Period.

Period.toString

Outputs this period as a String, such as P6Y3M1D. The output uses the ISO-8601 period format. A zero period is represented as P0D.

Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions

CHECKED VS UNCHECKED EXCEPTIONS

Errors and RuntimeExceptions are considered unrecoverable, while the rest, meaning checked exceptions, are considered recoverable.

Here, recoverable essentially means whether they should be caught using a try/catch block instead of letting them propagate up the call stack to the JVM.

There are multiple viewpoints regarding checked and unchecked exceptions.

As per the official Java tutorial: 

If a client can reasonably be expected to recover from an exception,
make it a checked exception.

If a client cannot do anything to recover from the exception,
make it an unchecked exception.

Another way to look at exceptions is to see whether the cause is internal or external to the program's code.

For example, incorrectly written code may try to access a reference pointing to null, or it may try to access an array beyond its length. These are internal sources of exception.

Here, using runtime exceptions is appropriate because ideally these problems should be identified while testing and should not occur when the program is ready for deployment.

On the other hand, a program interacting with files may not be able to do its job at all if a file is not available, but it should anticipate this situation. This is an external source of an exception and has nothing to do with the program's code itself.

It is therefore appropriate to use a checked exception in that kind of case.

Serialization Fields Memo

SERIALIZATION FIELDS MEMO

  • instance fields → restored from serialized data
  • static fields → not restored, taken from current class state
  • transient fields → also not restored, unless handled manually
Array print / toString notes

ARRAY PRINT / TOSTRING NOTES

You may find a few simple questions in the exam that expect you to know what is printed when you pass an array to System.out.print or System.out.println.

All you need to know is that when the class, or the superclass, of an object does not override toString(), Object's toString() is used. It prints: 

class name + @ + hash code

In the case of an array, the class name uses a special internal format.

The internal form of the name consists of the name of the element type preceded by one or more [ characters representing the depth of the array nesting.

ELEMENT TYPE ENCODING

boolean  -> Z
byte     -> B
char     -> C
class/interface -> Lclassname;
double   -> D
float    -> F
int      -> I
long     -> J
short    -> S

Note the L for class or interface types.

EXAMPLES

The name of a one-dimensional byte array is [B. So printing it gives something like: 

[B@<hashcode>

The name of a two-dimensional byte array is [[B. So printing it gives something like: 

[[B@<hashcode>

EXAM MEMORY

  • print(array) does not print the contents
  • it uses default Object.toString() behavior if not overridden
  • array type names use internal encodings like [B, [I, [[B
Java Text Blocks Notes

JAVA TEXT BLOCKS NOTES

The Java text blocks feature, standardized in Java 17, makes it easier to write compile-time constant strings within Java code.

Instead of writing:

String templateHtml =
"<html>\n"+
"   <body>\n"+
"      hello\n"+
"   </body>\n"+
"</html>\n";

You can write:

String templateHtml = """
   <html>
      <body>
         hello
      </body>
   </html>
   """;

The text is now more readable, and you do not need to write \n for line breaks.

RULES TO INTERPRET JAVA TEXT BLOCKS

DELIMITERS

  1. The starting delimiter is """ followed by optional whitespace and then a required ASCII LF new line character.
  2. The ending delimiter is """. In the example above, the String starts with <html> and ends with a new line character after </html>.

INDENTATION

  1. Leading whitespace used only to indent the text block is removed from each line. This is called incidental whitespace. Any whitespace remaining before the first non-whitespace character is essential whitespace and is kept.
  2. All trailing whitespace is removed, and each line is terminated with a single ASCII LF character. Even on Windows, where the source may use \r\n, Java normalizes it to \n.

ESCAPE CHARACTERS

You can still use escapes inside a text block. Example:

String s = """
Hello\tTab\n""";

\t inserts a tab and \n inserts a new line.

Usually, instead of \n, you can simply write the new line directly:

String s = """
Hello\tTab
""";

If you want to split a long line in the code without inserting a real new line in the resulting String, use \: 

String s = """
Hello \
World""";
System.out.println(s); // prints Hello World

Even though the code spans two lines, there is no new line between Hello and World in the String.

USEFUL EXAMPLES FOR THE EXAM

String s =
"""
hello
""";

This starts with h and ends with a new line character. Length = 6. Equivalent to: 

String s = "hello\n";
String s =
   """
      hello
   """;

Essential whitespace length is 3. Total length = 9. Equivalent to: 

String s = "   hello\n";
String s = """
      hello
      """;

Essential whitespace length is 0. Total length = 6. Equivalent to: 

String s = "hello\n";
String s = """
      hello""";

Essential whitespace length is 0 and there is no trailing new line. Total length = 5. Equivalent to: 

String s = "hello";
String s = """
                """;

This is an empty String. Length = 0. 

String s = """      hello
           """;

This does not compile because a new line is required after the opening """.

Pattern Variable Scope

PATTERN VARIABLE SCOPE

The scope of the pattern variable is a bit different from other scopes such as method scope. It has flow scope, which means it is in scope only in the path where the compiler is sure that it is reachable and also has a value.

For example, in case of an if statement, it is in scope only in the part where the result of the instanceof expression is true. It is not in scope in the else part and not in scope outside the if statement.

Note that not in scope is not the same as having a null value. Not in scope means that the variable itself is not available for use in code at that point.

Inside the if condition expression, it is in scope only if the compiler is sure that it has been assigned a value. For example: 

if (s instanceof String str && str.length() > 0)

Observe that && is a short-circuiting operator, which means the second part is evaluated only if the first part is true. Therefore, in the expression above, str is in scope in the second part and str.length() is valid.

The compiler knows that at this point str has definitely received a valid reference to a String instance. 

if (s instanceof String str & str.length() > 0) // invalid

Here, the second part of & is evaluated irrespective of the value of the first part. That means it is evaluated even if the first part is false.

But when the first part is false, str is not initialized. Therefore, the compiler is not sure that str definitely has a value at that point, and so str is not in scope there.
